I.

In the summer of 1977 the outer planets happened to line up in a way they had not since the age of Napoleon and would not again until the middle of the next century. Every 175 years or so, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune drift into a sequence that lets a single spacecraft tour them all, using each planet's gravity as a free throw. NASA, being lucky in its timing, built two machines and sent them out. Voyager 2 left first, on August 20. Voyager 1 followed on September 5, on a faster path that traded Uranus and Neptune for an early look at Saturn's smoggy moon Titan.

Bolted to the side of each spacecraft, outside the protective shroud, was a twelve-inch gold-plated copper record.

Think about what this object is. It is a phonograph record — a technology barely a century old at launch — plated in gold to survive radiation, sealed in an aluminum jacket, fitted with a stylus and engraved instructions, on the theory that a being with no ears, no hands, and no precedent for recorded sound might reverse-engineer music from first principles. On the cover is a diagram of the hydrogen atom, offered as a universal clock. There is a map anchored to fourteen pulsars — dead stars spinning like lighthouses — each labeled with its rotation period, so that a finder with a telescope could triangulate our sun from anywhere in the galaxy. Carl Sagan was asked to assemble the record, and he gathered a small committee — the astronomer Frank Drake, the writer Ann Druyan, the essayist Timothy Ferris, the artist Jon Lomberg, and Linda Salzman Sagan — and handed them one of the most absurd assignments ever given: summarize the planet. In the summer of 1977 the outer planets happened to line up in a way they had not since the age of Napoleon and would not again until the middle of the next century. Every 175 years or so, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune drift into a sequence that lets a single spacecraft tour them all, using each planet's gravity as a free throw. NASA, being lucky in its timing, built two machines and sent them out. Voyager 2 left first, on August 20. Voyager 1 followed on September 5, on a faster path that traded Uranus and Neptune for an early look at Saturn's smoggy moon Titan.

Bolted to the side of each spacecraft, outside the protective shroud, was a twelve-inch gold-plated copper record.

Think about what this object is. It is a phonograph record — a technology barely a century old at launch — plated in gold to survive radiation, sealed in an aluminum jacket, fitted with a stylus and engraved instructions, on the theory that a being with no ears, no hands, and no precedent for recorded sound might reverse-engineer music from first principles. Carl Sagan was asked to assemble the record, and he gathered a small committee — the astronomer Frank Drake, the writer Ann Druyan, the essayist Timothy Ferris, the artist Jon Lomberg, and Linda Salzman Sagan — and handed them one of the most absurd assignments ever given: summarize the planet.
